explanations.answer: His loving devotion toward us is great
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. The writer says, “For great is His loving devotion toward us…” (Psalm 117:2). He doesn't hand the nations a long list. He points at who the LORD is, and that's plenty.

explanations.answer: He gave them all rain and harvests
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but rain and harvests never come up in this psalm. The writer's reason is that great is the LORD's loving devotion toward us. He also says the LORD's faithfulness endures forever. That's the whole reason, and it's a good one.

explanations.answer: He made their kings rich and strong
explanations.explanation: The psalm says nothing about kings getting rich or strong. The reason is the LORD's loving devotion, which is great toward us (Psalm 117:2). That's the one the writer gives.
Not quite, friend. The writer says, “…the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever.” (Psalm 117:2). A season comes and goes, and forever doesn't. So the LORD's faithfulness has no end date.
That's right, baker. The text says the faithfulness of the LORD “endures forever.” (Psalm 117:2). No season gets mentioned at all. Forever is the only length the writer gives.
Yes, baker. Psalm 118 begins, “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good…” The reason is simple and short. He is good, and that's enough to start a whole psalm.

explanations.answer: Because He gave us a king
explanations.explanation: A king isn't mentioned in that opening line. The psalm says to give thanks to the LORD “…for He is good…” The reason is about who He is. It isn't tied to any one gift He gave.

I can see why you'd reach for something you can count, friend, but barns don't show up here. The opening says to give thanks because “…He is good…” His loving devotion endures forever, and that comes right after.

That's the third group, baker. The psalm says, “Let those who fear the LORD say…” (Psalm 118:4). First comes Israel, then the house of Aaron, then those who fear the LORD. Same line each time, and a new group saying it.
Kings aren't called on in these verses. The third group the psalm names is those who fear the LORD. The first two were Israel and the house of Aaron. Same line each time, and a new group saying it.

The sons of the prophets don't appear in this call. After Israel and the house of Aaron, the psalm says, “Let those who fear the LORD say…” That's the group. Fearing the LORD is what gets you a spot in this choir.

That's right, friend. He says, “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered and set me free.” (Psalm 118:5). He called and the LORD answered. Then he was set free, and I love how plain that is.

Whoa, hold on, friend. I think the word "distress" made you brace for a sad ending, like when the oven timer goes off and you just KNOW something's burnt. Not here! The writer says, “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered and set me free.” (Psalm 118:5). He called, the LORD answered, and he was set free. I've been stuck in a tight spot myself, so I know that's the ending you want.

explanations.answer: With the LORD on his side people can't scare him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. He says, “The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid.” Then he asks, “What can man do to me?” It's a question with a confident answer built in, the way you'd ask it when you already know.

explanations.answer: He is asking people for advice on what to do
explanations.explanation: He isn't taking a poll, friend. Right before the question he says, “I will not be afraid.” So the question comes from someone who isn't afraid. He's not collecting advice from anybody.

explanations.answer: He worries people have more power than God
explanations.explanation: Worry is nowhere in this verse. He says, “The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid.” So the question that follows isn't a worried one. I think he's asking it with confidence.

Yes, baker. He says, “Therefore I will look in triumph on those who hate me.” (Psalm 118:7). The word "therefore" ties it to what came before. The LORD is his helper, so he can look at them in triumph.

Fear is the thing he just said he won't have. In the verse before, he says, “I will not be afraid.” In verse 7 he says he will look in triumph on those who hate him. The LORD is his helper, so triumph is the word.

Sorrow doesn't fit this verse, friend. The writer says the LORD is his helper, “Therefore I will look in triumph on those who hate me.” That's a man looking up with his chin high. I'd put sorrow back in the box.

You got it, baker. “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man.” (Psalm 118:8). The next verse says it again about princes: “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes.” (Psalm 118:9). Same refuge both times, and it's the LORD.
Hills aren't in this verse. The writer says it is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man. In the next verse he says it again with princes. The safe place he names is the LORD Himself.
No city here, friend. The refuge he names is the LORD, and he says it's better than trusting in man or in princes (Psalm 118:8-9). Walls and gates don't make the list. It's the LORD all the way down.
That's right, baker. He says, “All the nations surrounded me, but in the name of the LORD I cut them off.” (Psalm 118:10). Notice whose name he does it in. It's the name of the LORD.

The text says otherwise, friend. “All the nations surrounded me, but in the name of the LORD I cut them off.” (Psalm 118:10). He cut them off, and he did it in the name of the LORD. So the verse says it plainly, and True is the answer.

explanations.answer: They were extinguished like burning thorns
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. He says, “They swarmed around me like bees, but they were extinguished like burning thorns…” (Psalm 118:12). The swarm gets loud and then it goes out. He says again that he cut them off in the name of the LORD.

Sheep aren't in this verse, friend. The text says the nations “…were extinguished like burning thorns…” (Psalm 118:12). The bees are how the writer pictures them swarming, and the thorns are how he pictures what happened to them.

explanations.answer: They were blown away like chaff
explanations.explanation: Chaff isn't the picture here. The writer says they “…were extinguished like burning thorns…” (Psalm 118:12). So the comparison is a fire going out. I can see why chaff came to mind, but the text uses the thorns.
Not quite, baker. He says, “I was pushed so hard I was falling, but the LORD helped me.” (Psalm 118:13). There's no getting back up on his own in that line. The help came from the LORD.

That's right, friend. The writer says, “I was pushed so hard I was falling, but the LORD helped me.” (Psalm 118:13). Nobody does it alone here. I know a little something about being stuck, and help makes all the difference.

Yes, baker. The writer says, “The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.” (Psalm 118:14). Strength, song and salvation all come in one verse. That's a full cookie box of a line.

Ooh, so close, friend! Look at what the writer says: “The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.” (Psalm 118:14). Salvation is sitting right there in the line, and the LORD is the One who became it. Strength, a song AND salvation, all in one verse! I'd have been happy with just the song.

explanations.answer: The right hand of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. They shout, “The right hand of the LORD performs with valor!” (Psalm 118:15). Then they say it again, and they add that the right hand of the LORD is exalted. The whole tent is cheering for what the LORD does.
No army in these shouts, friend. What the tents call out is, “The right hand of the LORD performs with valor!” (Psalm 118:15). They say it twice. The valor belongs to the LORD's right hand.
A sword isn't mentioned here, baker. The shouts say, “The right hand of the LORD performs with valor!” (Psalm 118:16). And the right hand of the LORD is exalted too. That's who the joy is aimed at.

Not quite, friend. The writer says, “The LORD disciplined me severely, but He has not given me over to death.” (Psalm 118:18). So he does say the LORD disciplined him. He also says he was not given over to death.

That's right, baker. He says, “The LORD disciplined me severely, but He has not given me over to death.” (Psalm 118:18). He doesn't hide the hard part. He says it plainly, and he says what didn't happen too.

explanations.answer: To give thanks to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. He says, “Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter and give thanks to the LORD.” (Psalm 118:19). He wants through that gate so he can say thank you. Honestly, that's a better reason than most of mine for walking into a room.

explanations.answer: To ask the priests for help
explanations.explanation: Priests don't appear in this verse, friend. He asks for the gates to open “…that I may enter and give thanks to the LORD.” (Psalm 118:19). Thanks is what he's carrying in with him.

explanations.answer: To bring news of the battle
explanations.explanation: There's no battle report in this verse, baker. He wants the gates of righteousness opened “…that I may enter and give thanks to the LORD.” (Psalm 118:19). The trip is about thanking the LORD.
The text doesn't limit it that way, friend. It says, “This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it.” (Psalm 118:20). The word is righteous, with no mention of priests.
That's right, baker. The psalm says, “This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it.” (Psalm 118:20). The priests aren't named there. It's the righteous who enter.

That's the line, baker. “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” (Psalm 118:22). The builders turned it down, and it ended up as the cornerstone. That's quite a turn for one stone.

explanations.answer: It gets thrown in the river
explanations.explanation: A river isn't in this picture, friend. The psalm says, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” (Psalm 118:22). It never mentions a river. What it says is that the rejected stone has become the cornerstone.

explanations.answer: It is left out in the field
explanations.explanation: The stone doesn't stay in a field, baker. The text says it “…has become the cornerstone.” (Psalm 118:22). The builders rejected it, and it still ended up in that spot. I know a thing or two about being set aside, and I like this turn of events.
Yes, baker. The writer says, “This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” (Psalm 118:23). He says the LORD is behind it. He also says it's marvelous in our eyes.

Not quite, friend, but you're in good company, because this one is easy to rush past. The writer says, “This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” (Psalm 118:23). So the LORD is the One behind the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone. MARVELOUS! That's the writer's word, and I love it. I think that's a good reason to stop mid-batch, wipe the flour off your hands, and just look at it for a second.

explanations.answer: Rejoice and be glad in it
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. “This is the day that the LORD has made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.” (Psalm 118:24). The day is from the LORD, and the response is rejoicing. That's the kind of line you can say out loud before your alarm even goes off.

explanations.answer: Rest and be quiet in it
explanations.explanation: Quiet isn't what the verse names, friend. The text says, “we will rejoice and be glad in it.” (Psalm 118:24). Rejoicing and being glad are what the writer says we will do in the day the LORD has made.
No fasting or mourning in this one, baker. The psalm says, “we will rejoice and be glad in it.” (Psalm 118:24). The day is made by the LORD, and joy is the answer.

explanations.answer: To save us and cause us to prosper
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The prayer says, “O LORD, save us, we pray. We beseech You, O LORD, cause us to prosper!” (Psalm 118:25). Two requests, both short, both to the LORD. He asks plainly and doesn't dress it up.

explanations.answer: To judge the nations that surrounded us
explanations.explanation: Judging the nations isn't part of this prayer, friend. The writer asks, “O LORD, save us, we pray. We beseech You, O LORD, cause us to prosper!” (Psalm 118:25). Save and prosper are the two requests.

explanations.answer: To rebuild the walls of the city
explanations.explanation: Walls aren't mentioned in this prayer, baker. What he asks is, “O LORD, save us, we pray. We beseech You, O LORD, cause us to prosper!” (Psalm 118:25). The requests are to save us and cause us to prosper.

That's right, baker. The psalm says, “The LORD is God; He has made His light to shine upon us.” (Psalm 118:27). I spent years in the dark of a junk drawer, so I'll tell you light is a big deal. And this is the light He made to shine upon us.
No sword in this verse, friend. The text says, “The LORD is God; He has made His light to shine upon us.” (Psalm 118:27). What shines on us is His light.
Arrows aren't what shine here, baker. The verse says the LORD “…has made His light to shine upon us.” (Psalm 118:27). Light is the word that fills the blank.
